_comment: Guided tour for colocalization in the emtk window. Steps point at real controls; the help page carries the long form.

steps.title: Every coefficient answers a different question
steps.text:
"Colocalized" is not one measurement. Pearson asks whether the two intensities co-vary; Manders asks whether they co-occur; M1 and M2 ask, separately, what fraction of each channel sits where the other is.

That last distinction is the one that gets lost: a protein can be 90 % colocalized with a marker while the marker is only 10 % colocalized with the protein, and a single Pearson number cannot say so.

Six steps, in the order that decides whether any of the numbers mean anything.

steps.title: Start with an image whose answer you know
steps.text: Load example writes a simulated two-channel image: channel A holds 14 bright discs, channel B holds the same 14 plus 14 more. So every disc of A has a partner in B (M1 ≈ 1), but only half of B sits on A (M2 ≈ 0.5), the asymmetry a single Pearson number cannot show. It also sets the thresholds; you press Run next.

steps.title: Run it and read the two Manders coefficients
steps.text: Run computes every coefficient for the selected pair. Read Manders M1 (A with B) and M2 (B with A): about 1 and about 0.5, with the threshold of 30 photons that sits between the background and the discs.

steps.title: Load your own image and name the two channels
steps.text: Two channels of the same field of view: a TIFF stack or a photon-stream file. Choosing or dropping a file loads and runs it. Which channel is A and which is B matters for M1 and M2 — they are not symmetric, and reporting one without saying which channel it belongs to makes it unreadable.

steps.title: Check the registration before anything else
steps.text:
The van Steensel CCF shifts channel B horizontally and recomputes Pearson at every offset:

• a peak at shift 0 — the channels are registered and the correlation is real;
• a peak away from 0 — chromatic aberration or a misaligned detector, and every coefficient is meaningless until you fix it;
• a flat profile — there is no spatial relation at all.

This is first for a reason. A registration error of one pixel can turn genuine colocalization into apparent exclusion, and nothing downstream will tell you.

steps.title: Thresholds decide Manders entirely
steps.text:
Pearson subtracts the means and is relatively forgiving. Manders does not — M1 and M2 are fractions of intensity above a threshold, so the threshold is the measurement, and changing it changes the answer without changing the data.

Auto-thresholding gives a reproducible starting point. Whatever you use, use the same rule for both channels and for every image in the comparison — and say what it was. A Manders coefficient without its threshold is not a number anyone can check.

Background subtraction comes first, for the same reason: an offset that is not removed sits above the threshold everywhere and inflates co-occurrence over the whole field.

steps.title: Ask whether it beats chance
steps.text:
A high coefficient on a densely labelled image can arise from nothing but the fact that both channels fill the field. The randomisation test asks the question directly — scramble one channel's blocks and recompute — and gives the coefficient a null distribution to be compared against.

Report the coefficient with that comparison. "PCC = 0.6" and "PCC = 0.6, above the 99th percentile of randomised images" are very different claims.

steps.title: And if the signal is punctate, count instead
steps.text:
Pixel-wise correlation assumes the signal fills space in a way that can co-vary. Punctate signal breaks that assumption: two sets of spots that never quite overlap correlate at nearly zero even when every spot has a partner a pixel away, because the correlation is computed pixel by pixel and the spots are narrower than their separation.

For puncta, count objects and their overlaps rather than correlating pixels — and use a region to restrict the analysis to the cell rather than the whole field, since empty background contributes agreement that is about the background, not the biology.

The Help button has the rest.
